title: Regret Is Weighted Forgetting
content: How much of a reinforcement learning agent's regret comes from its representation, and how much from its policy? Assume a representation $M$ clusters histories together into representational cells, discarding whatever set them apart. A policy must answer questions about histories, weighted by question frequency and history importance, and can give only one answer per cell, so merging incurs irreducible loss. This loss, together reducible error from bad decisions, is the quantity called regret. Here I show minimising regret means choosing what to represent, not only how to act. I prove least normalised regret equals $K_\rho(M)$, the weight deleted to leave one correct answer per cell. In a stripped-back setting $K_\rho(M)$ is freedom destroyed, where freedom measures how many further commitments a policy leaves open while staying correct. This ranks representations, and generalisation to unseen demands subsequently has probability $e^{-K_\rho(M)}$. I test this using Proximal Policy Optimization experiments, where a $K_\rho$ selector uses unlabelled target histories to choose among memory representations. Using $K_\rho$ reduced normalised regret by \( 8.4\% \) without target labels or rewards, against an impurity selector weighting within-cell conflicts equally. $K_\rho$ closed \( 95\% \) of the oracle-to-random selector gap, against \( 63\% \) for impurity. This bridges reinforcement learning and Stack Theory, a formalism of embodied generalisation-optimal learning, and demonstrates a practical use case.
